newsitem.title: USA: U.S. farmers seen planting 81-82 mln acres of corn.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farmers seen planting 81-82 mln acres of corn.

text.p: U.S. farmers will likely boost corn plantings to 81 million to 82 million acres this year from 79.5 million last year, grain market analysts said.
Much of the increase will be seen in the eastern Corn Belt, with corn reclaiming acres lost last year to soybeans due to heavy spring rains in Indiana and Ohio, they said.

"We're looking for the eastern Corn Belt to rotate those bean acres they were forced to plant because of floods, back to corn," said Bill Biedermann, vice-president of research at Allendale Inc in Illinois.
"At this point we're ballparking 82 (million acres), based on research done in October and November," Biedermann said.
The rains delayed planting well into June last spring, past the usual deadline for seeding corn in Ohio and Indiana.
"After last year in Indiana when we had such horrible weather, if we have decent weather you're going to see a lot of corn acres put in," said Joe Miller, market analyst at the Indiana Farm Bureau.
"Farmers are planning earlier this year," Miller added. "I've got farmers talking about planting already. After last year, they're itchy."
Miller said he expected U.S. acreage to top 81 million acres with Indiana's share between 5.3 and 5.5 million acres.

The U.S. Agriculture Department said at its Outlook Conference this week it expects plantings to reach 81 million acres this year. The National Corn Growers Association also chose that figure at a conference this week in Tampa, Fla.
However, analysts said planting intentions in the western Corn Belt were less clear than in the east.
Corn will compete fiercely with soybeans for new acres, with weather rather than price likely the determining factor for farmers, said Iowa-based agricultural consultant, Doug Hjort.
New crop soybeans at the Chicago Board of Trade were worth 2.5 times as much as new crop corn as of Friday, with November beans trading at $7.03 a bushel and December corn at $2.81.
"We need to see that at 2.8 or better before price is going to be a significant factor," Hjort said.

Analysts said a ratio above 2.5 to 1.0, premium soybeans, would ordinarily favor soybean plantings over corn. But many farmers had already applied fertilizers or purchased seed so it would take a sharp price move to change their intentions. Corn can be used on-farm, while soybeans are a pure cash crop.

"From this point forward, unless price moves drastically or unless weather forces a decision, prices aren't going to affect plantings all that much," said Dale Durchholz, analyst at AgriVisor Services, a division of the Illinois Farm Bureau.
"Fertilizer had been applied, people already have seed ordered," Durchholz added. "I think 81 to 82 million (acres) is really in the hunt."
A spokesman for Dekalb Genetics Corp confirmed seed sales were in line with plantings near 81 million acres.
"We're seeing our demand with the corn seed consistent with the 80 to 82 million acres that USDA is reporting," the spokesman said. "Our sales are at least that strong."
